headline: Rare White 'Ghost' Lobster Joins Maine Research Program
meta_description: A 1-in-100-million white lobster named Casper is helping scientists unlock the genetic secrets of rare lobster coloration at University of New England.
summary_short: Casper, a extraordinarily rare white lobster, has arrived at Maine's Marine Science Center to help researchers solve the mystery of unusual shell colors.
body:
A white lobster so extraordinarily rare that finding one occurs roughly once in every 100 million animals has arrived at the University of New England's Marine Science Center in Maine, where it will contribute to groundbreaking genetic research. Named Casper, the crustacean was donated by the Maine State Aquarium in Boothbay and will allow researchers to study the rarest coloration in the spectrum of unusual lobster shell colors. The university's noninvasive study, led by Professor Markus Frederich, aims to uncover why some American lobsters develop dramatically different colors from their species' typical mottled brown appearance. Casper's genetic material will be collected without harm to the animal as part of the effort.

The research program, launched in 2024, gained momentum after an orange lobster named Peaches—itself a 1-in-30-million rarity—produced offspring in a range of colors from typical brown to orange and blue. This unexpected family gave scientists a rare window into how coloration might be inherited. Researchers have already collected genetic samples from those juvenile lobsters and are analyzing more than 15,000 genes to identify which variations are associated with shell color changes.

Casper's arrival marks a significant milestone for the team. The white lobster's donation was coordinated by University of New England alumna Rue Motulsky, whose work on the DNA project as a student has already yielded new insights into lobster coloration. As Professor Frederich noted, these rare animals captivate people precisely because of their beauty and scarcity—but they also open doors to fundamental biological questions that advance our understanding of genetics and evolution in ways typical specimens simply cannot.
